Posted March 19, 2001
(MarijuanaNews note: " Bad journalism " really is the best two-word explanation for marijuana prohibition. What we have here are two examples, one from DEAland and one from Canada.
See
Marijuana Prohibition, Media Criticism, Copyrights and the 8th and 9th Commandments. By Richard Cowan

The first, from ABC, is a blatant fraud. It talks about a " debate " and then quotes only hard-line prohibitionists, not even moderate prohibitionists! Moreover, it quotes Barry McCaffrey as an infallible source on numbers that have no basis in fact.

The second item is a classic from the Calgary Sun, one of the worst papers in Canada. This piece is just rah-rah for marijuana prohibition and " if a nark said it, it must be true " reporting.)

Drug Demand Sparks Drug War Debate
From ABC News
See
Prime Time Live's " Junior High " Journalism

By Pierre Thomas
March 16, 2001
http://www.abcnews.go.com/
http://www.abcnews.go.com/onair/email.htm
http://www.abcnews.go.com/sections/wnt/DailyNews/wnt010316_drugwars.html

The War Over the Drug War

Though reports show that illegal drug use in the United States is half what it was in 1979, Americans are still spending billions to keep drug dealers in business.

Office of Drug Control Policy statistics say Americans are spending approximately $65 billion a year to buy illegal drugs.
(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, it is the Office of National Drug Control Policy.)

The drug-related damages amount to an estimated $110 billion a year, and approximately 52,000 deaths a year are drug-related.

While progress has been made in the war on drugs, law enforcement officials admit that these figures show that U.S. demand for drugs is still strong, making drug cartels apparently as powerful as ever.

" In many ways, we are seeing the most violent, well-funded criminal organizations global law enforcement has ever confronted, " said Gen. Barry McCaffrey, former White House director of the office of drug control policy.

Drug Arrests vs. Treatment

Over the past decade, law enforcement officials have adopted a hard-line " get tough " approach to drug trafficking, arresting an unprecedented number of drug offenders and giving them longer prison sentences. Between 1990 and 1998, according to the Bureau of Justice Statistics, the number of drug offenders in state prison doubled to 236,000. In addition, authorities have increased efforts to block drugs' entrance into the United States.

In 1999, police seized 2.6 million pounds of marijuana, heroin and cocaine that traffickers tried to bring into the country.

Copyright: 2001 ABC News Internet Ventures

From The Calgary Sun
callet@sunpub.com
http://www.canoe.ca/OttawaSun/home.html
March 17, 2001
By Peter Smith
(MarijuanaNews note: Peter Smith has given us other little gems.)
See
Article From The Calgary Sun Is So Dumb That Reading It Could Cause Brain Damage.
Prohibitionist Drivel At Its Worst.

High goal for drugs
(MarijuanaNews note: There really is an active debate in Canada about the future of marijuana prohibition, but the Calgary Sun just follows the party line.)
Police unit sets quota of $1M a month in pot busts

City police drug-unit pot busters have been ordered to hit a new quota of wiping out $1-million worth of marijuana a month.

And the new blitz is already ringing alarm bells among the city's huge army of basement pot growers.

Last week alone, city police and RCMP drug busts took $2-million worth of drugs off the streets.

" That's $2 million in one day in the city of Calgary, " said Det. Gord Renke, who is in charge of the four-man marijuana " green team " within the drug unit.
See
Half of Calgary " Green Team " Being Reassigned To Hard Drugs;
End of Civilization Anticipated By Local Narcs

" We never actually know the full extent of the effect we're having. " Police believe there's at least $20 million worth of pot under lights in city basements, but the figure could be much more.
(MarijuanaNews note: None of the numbers make any sense, but that is immaterial. Facts are obviously irrelevant here.)

At least 200 potential drug-growing houses have been reported to police, but no one knows how many more are unreported.

The drug unit's four-man, marijuana-busting " green team " spearheads the uphill fight, but even their $1-million-a-month quota can only take out 120 operations in a year.

Some may be as small as $70,000 busts, but many will rival two huge busts last week, when $500,000-pot-growing operations were dismantled.

Some criminals at the lower end of the organized crime scale keep their growing operations smaller so they won't get hit so hard by the courts when they're caught.
(MarijuanaNews note: Notice the premise is that everyone is involved in organized crime. In fact, most of the small growers are just small growers.)

And a few pot growers are set up to start a new operation as soon as their existing one is wiped out by police.

One grower had a fake wall in his basement with equipment for a marijuana-growing operation hidden behind it, aiming to start growing again immediately police cleared out his first operation.

Eagle-eyed police saw the fake wall and took away both grows.

Calgary's growers have a high reputation in the drug world, with one pound of Calgary marijuana worth one pound of California cocaine on the U.S. black market.
(MarijuanaNews note: Bingo! Classic party line. However, the RCMP web site says, " Many Canadian traffickers obtain their cocaine solely from US sources. Canadian marihuana is sometimes used as a currency to purchase cocaine that is warehoused in the USA. The exchange ratio is about 3 to 1.

Exchanges of 1 to 1 have been rumored but never substantiated. Furthermore, such a rate of exchange does not make sound commercial sense considering that a kilo of cocaine sells for $13,000 US (in lots of 50 kilos or more) while the wholesale price of a kilo of marihuana ranges around $6,000 or $8,000 US.


" It's because they've got so much coke down there and we've got so much pot up here, " Renke said.
